theme: Save me, O God; reproach has broken my heart
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 69:1-21. It is a cry of deep suffering from one who is hated for the sake of God. Notice how often the New Testament quotes this psalm.
settingTheScene: Psalm 69 is a psalm of David. It is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, second only to Psalm 22. The psalmist is sinking in deep waters, exhausted from crying, and hated without cause. What makes his suffering unusual is that it comes because of his zeal for God. It pairs well with Isaiah’s Servant, who suffered on behalf of others. It will appear again in Unit 18 with a different focus.
observation: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck” (v. 1).
“I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold” (v. 2).
“More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause” (v. 4).
“What I did not steal must I now restore?” (v. 4).
“For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face” (v. 7).
“I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s sons” (v. 8).
“For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me” (v. 9).
“They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink” (v. 21).
interpretation:
The opening images are those of drowning: deep waters, mire, floods. The psalmist is worn out with calling for help, his throat parched, his eyes failing from waiting for God. The suffering is intense, and it appears to come from several sources: false accusations, the loss of family, the mockery of those at the gate and the drunkards’ songs.

The unusual feature is the reason for it. “For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach.” His loyalty to God has made him a target. His zeal for God’s house has consumed him, and the insults aimed at God have landed on him. He has fasted and wept, and been mocked for it. There is no sense that the suffering is deserved. Though he acknowledges that he is not without folly (v. 5), the accusation against him is false.

The prayer turns on God’s steadfast love. “But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me.” He asks God to rescue him from the mire, and he appeals to God’s goodness: “Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good; according to your abundant mercy, turn to me.” Then comes the heartbreaking description of verses 20 and 21: “Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.”

This psalm helps us see the Servant’s suffering from the inside. The Servant is despised and rejected, with no one to comfort him. Yet the psalm leaves us with a question: what should the sufferer do? His answer is to pray. He does not repay hatred with hatred but brings his anguish to God. For the believer who suffers for righteousness’ sake, the psalm is a guide and a comfort.
connection: John 2:17 quotes verse 9, “Zeal for your house will consume me,” when Jesus cleansed the temple. John 15:25 quotes verse 4, “They hated me without a cause.” Romans 15:3 quotes verse 9, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me,” about Christ. Matthew 27:34, 48 and John 19:28-29 record the sour wine on the cross. Acts 1:20 quotes verse 25 in connection with Judas. 1 Peter 4:14 says that if we are insulted for the name of Christ, we are blessed.
application:
If you are suffering for doing right, bring it to God in honest prayer, and do not repay evil for evil.

Ask for the same zeal for God’s house that Jesus had, a love for the church that is real and costly.

Look for someone who has “looked for pity and found none.” Be the comforter.
prayerPrompts: Cry out to God about what overwhelms you.
Thank Jesus for the zeal that consumed him.
Ask him to teach you to bear reproach for his sake.
